To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: statistical_test

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
apriori NA 36 0.05 0.95 0.25 Cohen’s f G*Power
text
Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2007), at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design). Therefore, forty-eight participants were recruited to achieve a fully counterbalanced order of experimental conditions. Participants were recruited via a convenience sampling method from the University of Leeds Driving Simulator database. However, eye tracking data from 4 participants were not recorded due to failure at the calibration stage. Data from 44 participants (20 female, 24 male) was used for the analysis. Participants ranged in age from 25 to 63 years old (M = 40.23; SD = 11.19) and held a valid UK driving license for at least 3 years (M = 19.30; SD = 12.24). Their annual mileage ranged from 3000 to 18000 miles (M = 8125; SD = 3313), and they had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. The study was granted ethical approval from the University of Leeds Ethics Committee (BESS + FREC 2023 -0792 -877). Participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the experiment (both in verbal and written format, i.e., signing a consent form), and strict protocol was in place to make sure standardised instructions were provided to all participants. Data collection period spanned between 30 October 2023 to 23 November 2023.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 32 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p > .05 Based on the model prediction, participants reduced their glance time towards the forward roadway area in L2 assisted driving No significant main effect of lighting conditions was found for the percentage of glance time towards any of the four AOIs (p > .05).
p > .05 There was also no significant interaction effect across the four experimental conditions for the percentage of glance time towards any of the four AOIs (p > .05).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 7 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 7 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 11 distinct packages/libraries: dplyr, emmeans, ggplot2, glmmTMB, lme4, lmerTest, performance, readxl, stats, tidyr, viridis. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 153 columns across 5 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 7 R code files.

Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, source() call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

5 Percentage of Glance Time towards Right Periphery.Rmd — none
6 SD OF HORIZONTAL GAZE.Rmd — none
7 SD OF VERTICAL GAZE.Rmd — none

File paths

7 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: C:\\Users\\tsytl\\Desktop\\SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx to ../DataForAnalysis/SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx (in Attention towards the different types of ambient traffic.Rmd); C:\\Users\\tsytl\\OneDrive - University of Leeds\\Paper 2 - Visual Scanning Patterns\\PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx to ../DataForAnalysis/PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx (in Percentage of Glance Time towards Forward Roadway.Rmd); C:\\Users\\tsytl\\OneDrive - University of Leeds\\Paper 2 - Visual Scanning Patterns\\PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx to ../DataForAnalysis/PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx (in Percentage of Glance Time towards Instrument Cluster.Rmd); C:\\Users\\tsytl\\OneDrive - University of Leeds\\Paper 2 - Visual Scanning Patterns\\PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx to ../DataForAnalysis/PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx (in Percentage of Glance Time towards Left Periphery.Rmd); C:\\Users\\tsytl\\OneDrive - University of Leeds\\Paper 2 - Visual Scanning Patterns\\PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx to ../DataForAnalysis/PERCENTAGE OF GLANCE TIME ON EACH AOI.xlsx (in Percentage of Glance Time towards Right Periphery.Rmd); C:\\Users\\tsytl\\OneDrive - University of Leeds\\Paper 2 - Visual Scanning Patterns\\SD OF GAZE.xlsx to ../DataForAnalysis/SD OF GAZE.xlsx (in SD OF HORIZONTAL GAZE.Rmd); C:\\Users\\tsytl\\OneDrive - University of Leeds\\Paper 2 - Visual Scanning Patterns\\SD OF GAZE.xlsx to ../DataForAnalysis/SD OF GAZE.xlsx (in SD OF VERTICAL GAZE.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 7 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2007), at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design).

Therefore, forty-eight participants were recruited to achieve a fully counterbalanced order of experimental conditions.

Participants were recruited via a convenience sampling method from the University of Leeds Driving Simulator database.

However, eye tracking data from 4 participants were not recorded due to failure at the calibration stage.

Participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the experiment (both in verbal and written format, i.e., signing a consent form), and strict protocol was in place to make sure standardised instructions were provided to all participants.

Participants completed four experimental drives, presented in a counterbalanced order, with a 5-minute break after every two drives.

For the manual driving conditions, participants were told that they had full control of the movement of the car, and they were instructed to follow the traffic rules as they would when they were driving in a real urban setting with a speed limit of 30 mph.

During these conditions, participants were first exposed to one minute of manual driving before the system became available.

When the system first became available, an auditory message “Automation Available” was presented, and participants were instructed to engage with the system as soon as possible by pressing a specified button on the steering wheel.

For this reason, participants were required to monitor the road environment at all times and take over manual control if necessary by pressing the specified buttons on the steering wheel or turning the steering wheel for more than 2 degrees or pressing the brake pedal.

Upon arrival, participants were briefed on the experimental procedure and allowed to ask any questions they might have regarding the experiment before providing their consent.

Participants completed a series of self-report measures to provide their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles prior to the experimental drives (data are not reported in this manuscript).

Participants were accompanied by the experimenter during these drives.

Participants completed four experimental drives on their own, each of which lasted approximately 9 minutes.

Once all experimental drives were completed, participants were once again asked to complete a series of self-report measures to report their perceived driving skills, difficulties associated with driving after dark and their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles (data are not reported in this manuscript).

Participants were then debriefed and compensated £30 for their time.

Also, for practical reasons, participants took part in this driving simulator study during daytime hours, which limits our understanding of how circadian rhythms may have affected driver fatigue and influenced performance.

Ethics approval statement:

The study was granted ethical approval from the University of Leeds Ethics Committee (BESS + FREC 2023 -0792 -877).
