How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Driving Simulator Team at the University of Leeds for their dedication in creating the simulated driving environments. In addition, the authors would also like to thank Tobii for the use of the Tobii Glasses 3 for collecting the eye tracking data in the present study. Part of the findings of the present study will be presented at the 10 th International Conference on Driver Distraction and Inattention (DDI2026) at Gothenburg, Sweden.

1. Introduction

Vehicles equipped with assisted driving technologies such as SAE L2 (SAE, 2021) are now available to many consumers. These technologies provide support to drivers for both lateral and longitudinal movement of the vehicle. When L2 driving assistance is engaged, drivers are no longer involved in the moment-to-moment physical control of the vehicle. However, they are required to stay engaged in the driving task, by monitoring both the road environment and the assistance systems, to identify any potential system limitations (SAE, 2021), intervening if they identify a situation that cannot be handled by the system and could lead to a collision.

Previous studies have shown that drivers spend less time monitoring the forward roadway during L2 assisted driving, resulting a lower percentage of glance time towards road centre and increased visual attention towards areas away from the road centre (Gaspar & Carney, 2019; Pipkorn et al., 2024). This shift of visual attention may occur as drivers are no longer involved in the moment-to-moment control of the vehicle, thereby reducing the need for continuous monitoring of the forward roadway. In addition, when hands-off L2 is engaged, drivers show more extensive horizontal scanning of the driving environment (Louw & Merat, 2017), which may be advantageous for hazard detection (Mackenzie & Harris, 2015).

Assisted driving has also been shown to alter drivers' vertical gaze patterns. During uninterrupted motorway driving, Goncalves et al. (2020) found lower vertical gaze dispersion when L2 assisted driving was operational compared with manual driving, while Louw & Merat (2017) observed a similar pattern following an initial familiarisation period with the driving environment and the automated system. Drivers have also been found to devote less attention towards the dashboard area during uninterrupted urban driving under hands-off L2 assisted driving (Qin et al., 2025). However, the opposite pattern has been observed during transitions of control. During transitions of control, drivers require information both from the forward roadway and instrument cluster to acquire information about the disengagement of the driving assistance system, resulting in significantly higher vertical gaze dispersion when compared to manual driving condition (Goncalves et al., 2020).

While the aforementioned studies establish how the presence of L2 assisted driving alters gaze patterns, most evidence are primarily based on results from motorway settings and car-following scenarios (Louw & Merat, 2017; Morando et al., 2019; Morando et al., 2020; Morando et al., 2021; Pipkorn et al., 2024; Pipkorn et al., 2025), with relatively little focus on urban driving environment. Whether these insights could be extended to busy urban environment remains underexplored. Urban environments have a higher prevalence of peripheral hazards, including the presence of pedestrians and cyclists. Underwood et al. (2002) found that participants who watched video recordings of suburban scenes from a driver's point of view exhibited a greater dispersion of horizontal fixations, compared to motorway scenes.

Critically, the increased visual demand in an urban environment requires drivers to actively search for potential hazards, failure in doing so may delay hazard detection, resulting in a potential collision. The reduction in operational demands when L2 assisted driving is operational may facilitate such visual searching behaviours by freeing attentional resources for monitoring the driving environment. However, it remains unclear how visual attention is being reallocated during L2 assisted driving in complex urban environments.

Based on the STATS 19 database, driving after dark is associated with a higher percentage of road traffic collisions (RTC) (Fotios et al., 2021). One of the potential factors contributing to this heightened risk is the inherent difficulty in perceiving the driving environment in low visibility (Wood, 2020). This degradation can potentially increase drivers' reaction time for detecting hazards by up to 400ms, compared to optimal daytime conditions (Plainis & Murray, 2002). As drivers are allowed to engage L2 assisted driving systems after dark (Gershon et al., 2023), it is currently unclear how this would influence their visual scanning patterns and attention allocation across different Areas of Interest (AOIs) when the system is engaged.

Results from manual driving studies show that drivers adapt their visual scanning behaviour due to the visual challenges encountered after dark. Specifically, reduced visual acuity after dark may reduce bottom-up modulations of visual attention, as environmental stimuli become less salient. Consequently, drivers often exhibit a restricted distribution of fixations across the driving environment (Gruner & Ansorge, 2017) and are less likely to engage in mirror-checking behaviours (Urwyler et al., 2015). To compensate for this lack of visual acuity, drivers require a longer time to process visual inputs, once they are detected, leading to significantly longer fixation durations, compared to daytime conditions (Konstantopoulos et al., 2010; Urwyler et al., 2015). However, it is currently unclear how these visual scanning adaptations to reduced visibility in after dark driving conditions interact with the attentional reallocation associated with L2 assisted driving. Given that L2 assisted driving reduces drivers' operational demands from moment-to-moment basis, it may free attentional resources that could compensate for the increased attentional demands associated with reduced visibility in after dark driving environment.

A further consideration is that hazards in an urban environment take a variety of forms, with previous research suggesting that drivers may be more attracted to certain hazard types over others (Crundall et al., 2012). Specifically, Crundall et al. (2012) introduced the distinction between Behavioural Prediction (BP) and Environmental Prediction (EP) events. BP events involve road users whose actions can be directly observed and anticipated, such as a pedestrian visible at the roadside and walking towards the roadway. In contrast, EP events involve an object that obscures a driver's view of the surrounding environment (e.g., a parked vehicle), and drivers have to infer the probability of a hidden hazard emerging from it. It is argued that BP stimuli attract more attention compared to EP stimuli, because BP stimuli are directly observable, dynamic, entities that are more likely to trigger bottom-up attentional mechanisms.

Given that urban environments contain a variety of BP and EP elements, it remains unclear whether attention allocation towards these different types of ambient traffic varies across lighting conditions and levels of automation.

In light of the aforementioned research gaps, the present study explored drivers' visual attention allocation and scanning patterns, comparing manual driving and hands-off L2 assisted driving during uninterrupted driving in daytime and after dark conditions in an urban setting and explored whether different types of ambient traffic would trigger different attention allocation patterns across experimental conditions. The following research questions were proposed: 1.

How does drivers' visual attention allocation and scanning patterns differ between the two levels of driving (manual and assisted driving) and lighting conditions of the driving environment (daytime and after dark)? 2. How does drivers' visual attention allocation towards different element types differ across experimental conditions?

2. Methods

>Methods

2.1 Participants

Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2007), at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design). Therefore, forty-eight participants were recruited to achieve a fully counterbalanced order of experimental conditions. Participants were recruited via a convenience sampling method from the University of Leeds Driving Simulator database. However, eye tracking data from 4 participants were not recorded due to failure at the calibration stage. Data from 44 participants (20 female, 24 male) was used for the analysis. Participants ranged in age from 25 to 63 years old (M = 40.23; SD = 11.19) and held a valid UK driving license for at least 3 years (M = 19.30; SD = 12.24). Their annual mileage ranged from 3000 to 18000 miles (M = 8125; SD = 3313), and they had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. The study was granted ethical approval from the University of Leeds Ethics Committee (BESS + FREC 2023 -0792 -877). Participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the experiment (both in verbal and written format, i.e., signing a consent form), and strict protocol was in place to make sure standardised instructions were provided to all participants. Data collection period spanned between 30 October 2023 to 23 November 2023.

2.2 Apparatus

The study was conducted in a high-fidelity motion-based driving simulator -the second-generation University of Leeds Driving Simulator (UoLDS; see Figure 1). This included a Jaguar S-Type car, placed within a 4-metre spherical dome, with an operational steering wheel and pedals, providing a safe, highly immersive and controlled environment to analyse drivers' behaviour. Projectors equipped within the dome provided a 300-degree projection which displayed the driving environment. The head-mounted Tobii Pro Glasses 3 (Tobii AB, 2024) were used to collect gaze data.

This eye tracker collects gaze data at a 50 Hz sampling rate with an accuracy of 0.6 degrees and a precision of 0.03 degrees. It is also equipped with a scene camera, which records the driver's first-person view, providing a 106-degree diagonal field of view with a resolution of 1920 x 1080 gaze-overlapped video for post-processing.

2.3 Experimental Design

This study utilised a 2 x 2 within-participants design. The two main independent variables included were: level of automation (manual driving and hands-off L2 assisted driving) and lighting of the driving environment (daytime and after dark). Participants completed four experimental drives, presented in a counterbalanced order, with a 5-minute break after every two drives.

For the manual driving conditions, participants were told that they had full control of the movement of the car, and they were instructed to follow the traffic rules as they would when they were driving in a real urban setting with a speed limit of 30 mph.

2.4 Roadway Design

Participants drove along a two-lane urban roadway, with cars travelling in the oncoming lane at the rate of one car per kilometre. The urban environment was populated with ambient road users and static road elements, spaced equally every 40 metres and positioned randomly to the left and right of the driver. These included individually walking pedestrians approaching the roadway from the roadside, groups of talking pedestrians, standing cyclists, parked trucks, parked cars, bus stops (see Figure 2 for examples). These were positioned in equal proportions to the left and right, to avoid any biased visual attention allocation and scanning patterns to one location. For every drive, participants also encountered six actual or potential (materialised or non-materialised, respectively) hazardous events, including pedestrian crossing the road and oncoming vehicle turning across the path of the ego vehicle, some of which required resumption of manual control in the hands-off L2 conditions, to avoid a collision. However, the eye tracking and vehicle data associated with these events are reported in another manuscript (Lee et al., 2026).

2.5 The Driving Assistance System

For the L2 assisted driving conditions (SAE, 2021), the car was equipped with a driving assistance system that was capable of maintaining the vehicle within the driving lane and adhering to the speed limit (30mph). During these conditions, participants were first exposed to one minute of manual driving before the system became available. When the system first became available, an auditory message "Automation Available" was presented, and participants were instructed to engage with the system as soon as possible by pressing a specified button on the steering wheel. Once the system was engaged, drivers were asked to have their hands off the steering wheel and their foot off the pedals. However, the system was not be able to detect or respond to any hazardous events. For this reason, participants were required to monitor the road environment at all times and take over manual control if necessary by pressing the specified buttons on the steering wheel or turning the steering wheel for more than 2 degrees or pressing the brake pedal. If they resumed manual control to deal with a materialised or non-materialised hazardous event, they were told to re-engage the system as soon as possible, or the system would automatically re-engage after 10 seconds. All hazardous events were resolved within this 10-second window. The status of the driving assistance system was displayed on the Human Machine Interface (HMI) located in the dashboard area (see

2.6 Procedure

Upon arrival, participants were briefed on the experimental procedure and allowed to ask any questions they might have regarding the experiment before providing their consent.

Participants completed a series of self-report measures to provide their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles prior to the experimental drives (data are not reported in this manuscript).

They then took part in two practice drives (manual driving in after dark and L2 assisted driving in daytime environments) to familiarise themselves with the operational controls of the driving simulator. Participants were accompanied by the experimenter during these drives.

After the practice drives, calibration of the eye tracker was conducted, which was then repeated before every experimental drive.

Participants completed four experimental drives on their own, each of which lasted approximately 9 minutes. Once all experimental drives were completed, participants were once again asked to complete a series of self-report measures to report their perceived driving skills, difficulties associated with driving after dark and their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles (data are not reported in this manuscript). Participants were then debriefed and compensated £30 for their time. Based on the urban driving context, five main AOIs were specified: Forward Roadway, Left Periphery, Rear View Mirror, Right Periphery, and Instrument Cluster (see Figure 4). Forward Roadway covered the immediate forward roadway region from the driver's perspective, whereas the Instrument Cluster covered the speedometer and the HMI. The left periphery covered the regions within the leftward field of view from the driver's perspective, such as potential hazards on the left pavement, and the left-hand mirror. In contrast, the right periphery covered the regions within the rightward field of view from the driver's perspective, such as potential hazards on the right pavement, and the right-hand mirror. Gaze points that were not mapped onto these five main AOIs were classified as "Others", which included the sky and incabin areas. Four AOIs were considered for further analysis, with the "Rear View Mirror" and "Others" AOIs being exempted as drivers rarely glanced at these AOIs (on average, 0.91 % and 0.35 %, respectively across four experimental drives). Fixations were identified using the in-built Velocity-Threshold Identification Gaze Filter (I-VT filter) algorithm within Tobii Pro Lab, with a threshold of 100 degrees/second (Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000). Fixations with a minimum threshold of 100 milliseconds were filtered, which is consistent with previous studies with head-mounted eye trackers (Konstantopoulos et al., 2010; Urwyler et al., 2015). Glance-derived dependent variables were then constructed for each AOI to answer the research questions. A glance is defined as a sequence of consecutive fixations within the boundary of the same AOI, including all intervals in between (ISO, 2020; Morando et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2025; Seppelt et al., 2017).

2.7.2 Dependent Variables

Dependent variables considered in this study were the horizontal and vertical gaze dispersion, and percentage of glance time towards each AOI. Horizontal and vertical gaze dispersion were used to capture the spread of drivers' visual scanning patterns across the driving scene and were computed using the standard deviation of Gaze Point X and Gaze Point Y coordinates, respectively (Goncalves et al., 2020; Louw & Merat, 2017), in pixels. To capture how drivers distributed their overall visual attention across specific areas of the driving environment, percentage of glance time spent towards each AOI was calculated as the proportion of time spent glancing at each AOI relative to the total driving duration for the selected road segments (see Section 2.7.3), expressed as a percentage.

2.7.3 Selected Road Segments

To understand how drivers allocate their visual attention in an urban environment across different lighting conditions of the driving environment (daytime, after dark) and levels of automation (manual driving, hands-off L2 assisted driving), road segments containing oncoming cars and other ambient traffic were selected for analysis (see Section 2.4 for more details on the ambient traffic present). Only straight road segments were included to prevent the influence of road curvature on gaze behaviour. In addition, data from the road segments 100 metres before and 100 metres after each materialised and non-materialised hazardous event were excluded, to prevent drivers' reaction to those events from influencing the gaze behaviour (data associated with these hazardous events is reported in Lee et al., 2026).

2.8 Data Analysis

To answer the research questions, data were analysed using mixed-effects models (Stroup, 2012). All analyses were conducted using RStudio version 2025.5.0.496 (Rstudio Team, 2025). Model estimation was performed with the lmer and glmmTMB packages, and calculation of estimated marginal means (EMMs) and post-hoc comparisons were obtained through the emmeans package. All data and analysis code can be found on the repository: https://github.com/YeeThungLee/VisualScanningPatterns The fixed effects of the initial model included lighting of the driving environment (coded as 1 for daytime and 0 for after dark driving), the level of automation (coded as 1 for manual driving and 0 for hands-off L2 assisted driving, and the interaction between lighting conditions and level of automation. To account for potential order and learning effects, the run number (coded as 1 to 4) and the two-way interaction between run number and the independent variables were also considered. Participant ID was included as a random factor to account for individual differences.

A backward elimination method (James et al., 2021) was employed to refine the model by assessing its Akaike Information Criterions (AIC) values and the Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) to reduce the probability of overfitting and maintaining the model's parsimony. With this approach, a full model that consisted of all fixed effect factors mentioned in the previous paragraph was first considered. Factors associated with run number were eliminated one at a time if they did not contribute significantly to model fit, while retaining the key variables of the experiment, as they were not the primary factor of the experiment.

The model assumptions of the final fitted model were first evaluated prior to interpretation. Normality of residuals was evaluated by inspecting the Q-Q plot and assessed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test (Venables & Ripley, 2002). Homoscedasticity was examined via residuals against fitted value plots. For dependent variables where the assumptions were met, the analysis proceeded with the Linear Mixed Model (LMM; Stroup, 2012). For those cases where the assumption was violated, a Generalised Linear Mixed Model (GLMM; Stroup, 2012) was fitted, and EMMs were back-transformed to the response scale. The fixed effects variables retained in the final fitted model for each dependent variable, following backward elimination, are summarised in Table 1. The model fit indices for each mixed-effects model are also included in Table 1. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction were conducted, and the significance level was set at p < .05.

Out of 176 potential data points (44 participants x 4 experimental drives), some were excluded due to technical issues associated with the driving simulator or eye tracker, or because participants failed to follow the experimental protocol. The final analyses included 164 data points: 39 for hands-off L2 assisted driving in daytime and after dark conditions, and 43 for manual driving in daytime and after dark conditions.

To answer the second research question, regarding visual attention to different types of ambient traffic, two categories of ambient road elements were operationalised, based on the distinction proposed by Crundall et al. (2012): (1) the "Behavioural Prediction" (BP) element, which included the walking pedestrians and cyclist; and (2) the "Inanimate Object" (IO), which included the parked cars and trucks, which were static elements that could potentially occlude other road users from the driver's view. Given that no hazard emerged from behind the static elements in the present study, this category was termed differently from Crundall et al.'s (2012) "Environmental Prediction" (EP) element.

GLMMs were constructed to investigate whether these different elements elicited distinct attention allocation patterns across the various experimental drives. The dependent variable for these models was the mean glance duration towards the left and right peripheries to capture the amount of visual attention devoted to these areas of the driving scene. Rather than analysing the entire drive, this analysis focused exclusively on segments where either BP or IO elements were presented within those specified AOIs. The models were refined using a backward elimination process, where the three-way interaction was then excluded as it did not significantly improve the model fit (see Table 1 for the final retained fixed effects).

3. Results

>Results

3.1 Gaze Dispersion

As shown in Figure 5, the contour plots in L2 assisted driving panels showed a more concentrated vertical gaze pattern relative to that observed in manual driving conditions. This concentration was more evident in the marginal histogram for Gaze Point Y during L2 assisted driving during daytime condition, showing a narrow peak. In contrast, the marginal histogram for Gaze Point Y during L2 assisted driving after dark condition showed a distinct secondary peak, reflecting greater variability in vertical gaze locations. The main effect of level of automation on horizontal gaze dispersion was not found to be significant (F (1, 115.39) = 2.380, p = .126). As for vertical gaze dispersion, there was a significant main effect of level of automation (F (1, 118.73) = 245.931, p < .001). Based on the model predictions, vertical gaze dispersion was significantly reduced by 33.4% in L2 assisted driving (EMMs = 69.2 pixels, SE = 2.92) relative to manual driving conditions (EMMs = 103.9 pixels, SE = 2.87).

Both horizontal (F (1, 114.92) = 0.391, p =.533) and vertical gaze dispersion (F (1, 118.24) = 0.339, p = .562) were found to be similar across daytime and after dark driving environments.

No significant interactions were found for horizontal gaze dispersion (F (1, 114.92) = 0.145, p =.704). In contrast, a significant interaction was found between level of automation and lighting conditions for vertical gaze dispersion (F (1, 118.24) = 4.722, p = .032). Post-hoc comparisons showed that while L2 assisted driving consistently reduced vertical gaze dispersion compared to manual driving for both daytime and after dark lighting conditions, the magnitude of reduction was significantly more pronounced in the daytime (by 37.31%; t (118) = -12.636, p < .001; see Figure 6) than that observed in after dark conditions (by 29.19%; t (118) = -9.569, p < .001; see Figure 6). There was a significant main effect of run number on horizontal gaze dispersion (F (3, 115.08) = 5.280, p = .002). As shown in Figure 7, participants decreased their horizontal gaze dispersion from Run 1 to Run 3 (t (115) = 3.817, p = .001) and from Run 1 to Run 4 (t (115) = 2.817, p = .034).

3.2 Percentage of Glance Time towards each AOI

The results obtained from the mixed-effects model showed that there was a significant main effect of level of automation on the percentage of glance time towards the forward roadway AOI (F (1, 118.53) = 10.221, p = .002; see Figure 8). Based on the model prediction, participants reduced their glance time towards the forward roadway area in L2 assisted driving No significant main effect of lighting conditions was found for the percentage of glance time towards any of the four AOIs (p > .05).

There was also no significant interaction effect across the four experimental conditions for the percentage of glance time towards any of the four AOIs (p > .05). A significant main effect of run number was found on the percentage of glance time towards both the left (F (3, 116.51) = 10.167, p < .001) and right periphery (F (3, 115.22) = 12.094, p < .001).

As shown in Figure 9 (Left), post-hoc tests showed that participants significantly increased their glance time towards the left periphery from Run 1 to Run 2 (t (116) = -3.003, p = .020) and from Run 1 to Run 3 (t (116) = -5.001, p < .001). In contrast, participants significantly reduced their glance time towards the left periphery from Run 3 to Run 4 (t (117) = 4.148, p < .001).

For the right periphery AOI (see Figure 9 (Right)), participants reduced their glance time from Run 1 to Run 2 (t (117) = 4.537, p < .001) and from Run 1 to Run 3 (t (117) = 5.078, p < .001). In contrast, participants increased their glance time towards the right periphery from Run 2 to Run 4 (t (119) = -3.173, p = .012) and from Run 3 to Run 4 (t (118) = -3.702, p = .002).

3.3 Attention towards the different types of ambient traffic

To examine whether drivers allocated different levels of visual attention to Behavioural Prediction (BP) and Inanimate Object (IO) elements across experimental conditions, mean glance durations towards the left and right peripheral environments were analysed when these elements were present. Results showed that drivers allocated greater visual attention to BP elements than IO for both the left (z = 3.86, p < .001; see Figure 10) and right (z = 2.89, p = .004; see Figure 11) peripheral environments. For the left periphery, BP elements elicited significantly longer mean glance durations (EMMs = 845.95, SE = 41.51) than IO (EMMs = 685.66, SE = 34.78). This greater visual attention allocation towards BP elements at the left periphery was consistent across experimental conditions with no significant interactions seen between element type and lighting condition, or element type and level of automation.

For the right periphery, however, the difference in mean glance duration between BP and IO was moderated by lighting conditions (z = -1.97, p = .049). Post-hoc Bonferronicorrected comparisons showed that the BP elements elicited significantly longer mean glance durations than IO, only during daytime conditions (z = 3.39, p = .004), with no significant differences found after dark (p = 1.000). No significant interaction was found between level of automation and element type.

4. Discussion and Conclusion

This driving simulator study explored the effects of lighting conditions in the driving environment and levels of automation on drivers' visual attention allocation and scanning patterns. The study also investigated whether visual attention allocation towards different types of ambient traffic present in an urban environment (i.e., BP and IO) differed between manual driving and L2 assisted driving, for these different driving environments.

Contrary to previous findings (Louw & Merat, 2017; Mackenzie & Harris, 2015), our results showed that drivers had similar horizontal gaze dispersion patterns in manual and L2 assisted driving. This difference in findings from previous studies could be due to the urban traffic environment used in the present study, compared to use of car following tasks in a motorway scenario for previous studies. The regular presence of ambient urban traffic located in the peripheral areas may have consistently attracted drivers' visual attention, potentially resulting in high horizontal gaze dispersion, regardless of level of driving automation, with the motorway studies having comparatively less objects of interest in the peripheral areas, coupled with the need to focus on the lead vehicle, in case of an impending collision.

Although horizontal gaze dispersion did not differ between the two levels of automation, results from the percentage of glance time towards each AOI showed that drivers spent more time monitoring the left and right peripheral environments throughout the drive during L2 assisted driving, when compared to manual driving. This suggests that L2 assisted driving did not alter the overall horizontal extent of visual scanning, but it did increase the amount of time drivers spent monitoring both left and right peripheral regions of the driving environment throughout the drive. The reduced operational demand offered by hands-off L2 driving is thought to reduce workload, providing more resources for drivers to monitor their surroundings (De Winter et al., 2014; Mackenzie & Harris, 2015). Participants' visual attention allocation also evolved across runs, likely reflecting how they adapted to the driving environment. Participants initially devoted more attention to the left peripheral environment, as reflected by a higher percentage of glance time towards the left periphery, where potential hazards were closer to the ego vehicle, before increasing attention towards the right periphery in the later runs. This shift was accompanied by a reduction in horizontal gaze dispersion across runs, which suggests that drivers initially adopted a broader exploratory scanning strategy, and subsequently adapted their visual sampling behaviour as they became familiar with the driving environment.

Drivers' visual attention towards different types of ambient urban traffic within the peripheral environment varied, based on their nature. Regardless of level of automation, drivers spent more time looking at Behavioural Prediction elements (e.g., walking pedestrians and cyclists) relative to Inanimate Objects (e.g., parked trucks and parked cars). This finding aligns with Crundall et al. (2012) who found that BP stimuli attract more attention compared to static elements. This pattern may reflect the dynamic nature of the BP stimuli, which are more likely to trigger bottom-up attention mechanisms. In addition, pedestrians and cyclists pose a greater potential collision risk than parked vehicles, as they may be perceived as more likely to enter the roadway. This bias appeared to be robust across automation levels, suggesting that drivers continued to focus more on safety-relevant road users, as an attempt to anticipate potential hazards and maintain situation awareness.

Consistent with previous studies (Goncalves et al., 2020; Morando et al., 2019; Morando et al., 2020; Pipkorn et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). the vertical gaze dispersion seen during uninterrupted driving in hands-off L2 conditions was significantly lower than that observed for manual driving. This is because during manual driving, drivers are responsible for the moment-to-moment control of the vehicle, and visuomotor coordination remains intact (Mole et al., 2019). They are therefore required to acquire information from the forward roadway and instrument cluster to guide the car's trajectory and maintain its speed. This interpretation is also supported by the percentage of glance time data to each AOI, which showed that drivers had a lower percentage of glance time towards the instrument cluster and forward roadway during L2 assisted driving, compared to manual driving.

In terms of the effect of lighting on visual scanning patterns, the percentage of glance time towards the four AOIs and the horizontal and vertical gaze dispersion patterns were found to be similar for the daytime and after dark conditions. These results are consistent with those reported in a previous driving simulator study (Konstantopoulos et al., 2010). However, the lighting conditions of the driving environment in this study was found to moderate visual attention allocation on the different urban elements, shown in mean glance duration towards the AOIs when these elements were presented. Specifically, the greater visual attention allocation towards the BP elements, when compared to IOs, was only observed in daytime, especially for those items located in the right periphery. The absence of this difference in after dark may reflect a reduced ability to distinguish between BP and IO under reduced visibility, consistent with previous arguments that reduced saliency of environmental cues in after dark environments hinders drivers' ability to perceive and interpret road information (Wood, 2020).

This effect appeared to be particularly pronounced in the right periphery, potentially because the ego vehicle's headlamps primarily illuminated the forward roadway, and, to some extent, the left periphery, creating lower levels of luminance in the right peripheral space.

Consequently, drivers may have found it more difficult to distinguish between BP and IO elements in the right periphery, resulting in a non-significant difference in mean glance duration across the two element types in after dark.

L2 assisted driving reduced vertical gaze dispersion compared to manual driving; however, this reduction was less pronounced in the after dark lighting conditions. This pattern may be attributable to the reduced visibility of the after dark environment, which limits drivers' capability for detecting any ambient urban traffic in the far distance (Garay et al., 2004; Garay-Vega et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2026). As a result, ambient traffic only became visible at a closer distance in the after dark environment. As objects closer to the ego vehicle are projected lower in the visual field relative to the horizon line, drivers would be required to allocate their gaze across a broader range of vertical locations when monitoring the road environment, resulting in greater vertical gaze dispersion. Consequently, although L2 assisted driving reduced the necessity for downward gaze shifts towards the instrument cluster for speed-control purposes, drivers still needed to vertically distribute their gaze to sample the nearby roadway environment. This interpretation is consistent with the distinct secondary peak observed in the Gaze Point Y distribution during L2 assisted driving after dark, indicating greater variability in vertical gaze locations. Overall, these findings suggest that the effect of L2 assisted driving on visual scanning is not uniform across lighting conditions, with drivers appearing to adapt their visual scanning behaviours to meet the increased demands of reduced visibility after dark.

Future design of driving assistance system may be benefit from incorporating night-vision camera system to support better visual attention in reduced visibility environment.

4.1 Limitations and Future Work

One main shortcoming of this study is the use of a driving simulator to explore visual scanning patterns when driving after dark, which might not provide the same levels of luminance associated with driving at night in the real world (Wood & Chaparro, 2011). Also, for practical reasons, participants took part in this driving simulator study during daytime hours, which limits our understanding of how circadian rhythms may have affected driver fatigue and influenced performance. Therefore, further research is warranted to investigate how nighttime driving affects drivers' visual attention and scan patterns in a real-world urban environment, and how this is influenced by levels of automation, to improve ecological validity and a more holistic understanding of this topic.
